title: Non-vacuous behavioral certificates at frontier scale

concept.text: Proposed innovation: give a learned system with frontier task capability a machine-checked behavioral guarantee over a useful, explicitly defined deployment envelope. The certificate would establish that a stated safety or correctness property holds for every input covered by its assumptions. An alternative would certify every non-abstaining output and prove that the system abstains outside its certified region. The envelope would describe the operating conditions, input variations, shifts and interventions the guarantee covers.

Here, non-vacuous means that the guarantee preserves useful task performance and covers enough of the intended deployment to matter. A system that always abstains, returns a constant answer or certifies only an operationally negligible region would not fulfill the proposal. The innovation therefore combines three requirements: substantive capability, useful certified coverage and a checkable argument connecting the implemented system to its stated property. These are proposed requirements, rather than achievements established by the supplied evidence.

The supplied technical example illustrates a narrower form of certification: Chen and colleagues analyze a smoothed safety detector over specified perturbation neighborhoods. Their formulation seeks a bound covering all adversarial inputs within a declared distance, rather than relying solely on attacks that happened to be tried. This supplies a basis for understanding scoped behavioral guarantees, while leaving a substantial gap between a local detector certificate and the proposed guarantee for a complete capable system.

significance.text: Empirical testing establishes behavior on evaluated cases; a successful attack can expose a failure, but unsuccessful attacks need not establish that no failure exists. The paper explicitly notes that adversarial examples can remain undiscovered because attackers have limited time or information. A certificate instead aims to establish a specified property across its entire declared set, subject to its assumptions. This difference is the technical basis for assurance beyond observed benchmark or attack performance.

Conditional significance: if useful deployment coverage and frontier task performance could be combined with machine-checked guarantees, engineers could incorporate capable learned components while stating precisely which behaviors had been established under which conditions. The direct consequence would be assurance of the certified property within the certified envelope. Applications in medicine, aviation and other demanding settings could follow, but would still require appropriate specifications, integration with the surrounding system, validation and applicable approval. Certification alone would not establish readiness for those applications.

A certificate is only as relevant as its specification and assumptions. Proving the wrong property does not establish the intended safety outcome; proving a detector's robustness does not automatically establish the safety of every generated answer. Chen and colleagues distinguish these targets and explain that a practical bound may be unavailable for the broader output-safety formulation. The proposed advance would consequently require both a useful property and a proof that actually addresses the deployed behavior of interest.

Scope of the proposed impact: certification would not automatically explain training dynamics, predict what future training will produce or guarantee alignment with human values under arbitrary self-modification. Nor would a guarantee extend to unmodeled conditions merely because the certified system is highly capable. These limits keep the innovation focused on useful, explicit behavioral envelopes rather than an unrestricted promise of universal safety.

missing_breakthrough.text: The proposed missing capability is a specification class, training method, proof system or combination of these that makes useful behavioral certification tractable at frontier task capability. It must cover declared deployment shifts and interventions without reducing the system to a policy too limited to perform the task. The supplied paper documents a narrower demonstration and obstacles to scaling; it does not establish that this broader capability is absent throughout the field.

Computational tractability is one barrier. Chen and colleagues state that verifying ReLU networks is NP-complete, citing Katz et al. (2017), and describe scaling difficulties for the interval-bound-propagation methods they discuss. The Katz paper was not inspected in the supplied review, so the exact decision problem and its assumptions cannot be established here. This secondary statement should not be expanded into a claim that every property of every neural network is NP-complete, or that every restricted verification problem is impractical.

Preserving utility while obtaining strong bounds is another barrier. The paper describes a smoothness–utility trade-off: excessive smoothing can produce a constant output and destroy useful discrimination. Increasing a certified perturbation radius is also not an unlimited objective, because sufficiently small textual changes can legitimately change meaning and the appropriate safety judgment. A successful advance must therefore certify a property suited to the task, rather than obtain a large numerical radius by erasing distinctions the task requires.

Engineering synthesis: the remaining work includes expressing meaningful deployment conditions precisely, handling randomness and interventions explicitly, connecting the proof to the actual implementation and proving that any abstention mechanism obeys its advertised boundary. A neighborhood around benchmark prompts is not automatically a model of deployment. Likewise, a sound mathematical bound for a smoothed detector is not automatically a machine-checked guarantee for the complete system. These are requirements of the proposed innovation, not independently established impossibility results.

current_state.text: The supplied dated evidence is the 8 October 2025 version of Chen, Dong, Wei, Su and Zhu's arXiv paper, Towards the Worst-case Robustness of Large Language Models. Its reported certification focuses exclusively on a safety detector. The detector guarantee should be distinguished from a guarantee that every answer generated by an LLM is safe. The paper discusses a broader output-certification formulation, but the supplied review reports that a practical bound for that formulation may remain unavailable.

Table 2 reports an average certified token-level ℓ0 radius of 2.02 for a uniformly smoothed GPT-4o safety detector on AdvBench. This concerns token substitutions, rather than arbitrary text edits. It is an average across evaluated prompts, not a uniform radius promised for every prompt. The method uses sampled confidence estimates; the supplied review does not establish that the result is an inspected machine-checked proof or a deterministic guarantee about every generated answer.

The reported average certified suffix length of 6.41 has an unresolved model attribution. The abstract associates both 2.02 and 6.41 with GPT-4o, while Table 3 explicitly labels its suffix experiments as using Llama-3-8B and reports 6.41 for the uniform kernel at β = 0.25. The supplied evidence does not resolve that internal discrepancy. The number can be retained as a reported result, but cannot confidently be assigned to GPT-4o.

Table 1 reports 0–2% robustness for the tested deterministic defenses under the I²-GCG attack on three open models: the relevant entries are 0% except for a 2% result for PAT on Llama2-7B. These are attack-derived upper bounds in the reported experimental setup. They demonstrate serious weaknesses in those tested defenses, rather than proving that every deterministic defense fails or that defenses in other access settings are useless.

A mean radius near two token substitutions is local coverage, but its significance cannot be judged solely by its numerical size. Section 6.2 reports a human reference radius of 2.12 and discusses the possibility that perturbations change the correct judgment. This helps explain why larger radii need not always represent better task behavior. The local result remains scientifically meaningful, while falling short by itself of the proposed deployment-envelope demonstration.

The supplied review relied on a partial extraction that truncates during Appendix D.4, even though later limitations sections are listed. The source index records retrieval on 9 November 2026, but retrieval of a 2025 paper does not establish the field's subsequent state. The bounded freshness search record is empty, and no supplied source demonstrates the proposed completion capability. These limitations prevent a field-wide conclusion about its absence as of 1 November 2026; they do not invalidate the paper's dated results. No peer-review status or independent reproduction is established by the supplied materials.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: select a substantive task, such as control or triage, and pre-register the deployment envelope, safety or correctness property, task-performance metric, acceptable performance gap from an unconstrained frontier baseline and minimum useful certified coverage. The model should meet the declared performance gap without unreported human assistance. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established community standards; numerical thresholds should be justified by the chosen task.
completion_criteria.label: Preregister useful certification criteria and meet declared task performance

completion_criteria.text: Proposed proof requirement: supply a machine-checked argument that the stated property holds throughout the declared envelope. If the system uses abstention, prove that every non-abstaining output satisfies the property under the declared assumptions and that the system abstains outside its certified region. Evaluate the complete system, including abstentions, against both the performance and coverage requirements. This prevents an always-abstaining or almost-never-operating system from qualifying.
completion_criteria.label: Machine-check behavioral guarantees while meeting performance and coverage requirements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical and reproducibility requirements: specify covered shifts, interventions, randomness, implementation assumptions and any confidence qualifications. Make the model or precisely identified deployed system, specification, proof artifacts, checking procedure and evaluation protocol available sufficiently for independent scrutiny and reproduction. Report the operational cost of certification and abstention so that the claimed useful envelope can be assessed in practice. If access is restricted, state exactly which parts independent evaluators can reproduce.
completion_criteria.label: Provide reproducible certification artifacts, explicit assumptions, and operational costs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed adequacy boundary: a certificate covering an average radius of about two token substitutions, or a proof for a network unable to perform the substantive task, would not by itself meet this demonstration. Such results can remain valuable intermediate advances. Multiple independently reproduced tasks and environments would establish demonstrated breadth, while a proof would establish the stated property only within its formal scope. Neither finite testing nor success on several deployments would establish literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Establish substantive task certification while respecting formal scope limits

related_concepts.text: Title-based comparison with MLC-01, A predictive theory of what deep networks learn: predicting the outcome of training and certifying the behavior of an already trained system are different objectives. A certificate could apply even without a predictive training theory, while such a theory could help identify architectures or training procedures that are easier to certify. The supplied roster contains titles rather than full concept records, so this comparison does not establish their precise boundaries.

Title-based comparison with MLC-06, Algorithmic legibility sufficient to verify and edit a model: understanding a model's internal algorithms may help construct specifications and proofs, but an explanation of a circuit alone does not establish a behavioral property for every input in an envelope. Conversely, a behavioral certificate need not provide a complete explanation of the model's mechanisms. The entries retain distinct goals despite their substantial overlap around verification.

Title-based comparison with MLC-04, World models that survive novel interventions, and MLC-09, Skill learning from scarce, irreversible, real-world outcomes: intervention robustness could supply behavior worth certifying, while irreversible outcomes could make assurance before action particularly valuable. Demonstrating robust prediction or efficient real-world learning would not by itself prove a deployment-envelope property. Certification would need to state which interventions, actions and consequences its assumptions actually cover.

Title-based comparison with MLC-02, Domain learning at a human experience budget; MLC-03, Cumulative learning without forgetting or loss of plasticity; and MLC-05, Local credit assignment that matches backpropagation at scale: these concern how systems acquire or retain capability. MLC-10 concerns guarantees about the resulting behavior. Learning and editing may change the system to which a certificate applies, so extending assurance across updates would require an explicit argument; it cannot be inferred from learning efficiency, retention or a credit-assignment method alone.

Title-based comparison with MLC-07, Open-ended curricula that create externally verified new competencies, and MLC-08, Discovery of new empirical laws, confirmed by experiment: external evaluation and experimental confirmation can establish that a competency or discovery succeeds under tested conditions. A formal behavioral certificate addresses a different evidential target: a specified property throughout a declared set under explicit assumptions. These forms of evidence can complement one another without substituting for one another.

Title-based comparison with MLC-11, Frontier competence at a biological-order power budget: efficient computation could make a certified system more practical, but power efficiency does not establish behavioral correctness, and behavioral certification does not establish efficient operation. These remain separate innovations. The historical item 8 mentioned in the earlier research is absent from the supplied roster; its precise relationship cannot be reconstructed. The present concept's scope excludes a general guarantee of alignment under arbitrary self-modification.

unresolved_issues: The model responsible for the reported average certified suffix length of 6.41 remains unresolved because the abstract and Table 3 conflict.
The precise ReLU verification decision problem and assumptions behind the secondary NP-completeness attribution remain unverified.
The supplied evidence does not establish whether deployment-envelope certificates meeting the proposed requirements existed elsewhere as of 1 November 2026 or subsequently.
The retained extraction truncates during Appendix D.4; potentially relevant later limitations were not available in the supplied review.
The supplied materials do not establish peer-review status, independent reproduction or machine checking of the paper's reported certification arguments.
Task-specific definitions of frontier baseline, acceptable performance gap, useful coverage and practical certification cost remain to be chosen for any concrete demonstration.
Only roster titles were supplied for related concepts, and historical item 8 was not supplied; precise cross-entry boundaries remain provisional.

brief.title: Highly capable AI with proven limits on its behavior
possible: People could use AI for demanding tasks with a computer-checked proof that it meets a stated safety or correctness rule under clearly defined operating conditions. The guarantee would cover every input within those conditions, including specified changes.
An AI could instead guarantee every answer it gives and decline to answer outside the conditions its proof covers. It would still have to do useful work across enough of its intended use to matter.
why: Engineers could build capable AI into systems while knowing exactly which behaviors are guaranteed under which conditions. That would provide assurance beyond passing tests or resisting the attacks people have tried.

sources.who: Huanran Chen, Yinpeng Dong, Zeming Wei, Hang Su and Jun Zhu
sources.showed: They derived mathematical bounds for a safety detector that averages judgments over randomly altered text. Its average guaranteed range covered about two substitutions of tokens, the pieces of text a language model processes.
sources.quote: First, we upper bound the worst-case robustness of deterministic defenses using enhanced white-box attacks, showing that most of them achieve nearly 0% robustness against white-box adversaries.
sources.cited_for: The work shows how guarantees against specified text changes differ from testing particular attacks.
sources.not_established: A guarantee for a detector does not prove that a complete AI system always produces safe answers within useful operating conditions.

sources.who: Samuel Teuber, Stefan Mitsch and André Platzer
sources.showed: They linked proofs about safe control decisions to learned controllers and their physical surroundings. They proved safety without a time limit in some aircraft collision-avoidance scenarios.
sources.quote:
We prove
infinite-time safety on the classical Vertical Airborne Collision Avoidance NNCS
verification benchmark for some scenarios
sources.cited_for: Safety proofs can cover a learned controller together with the modeled physical system it controls.
sources.not_established: The demonstrated controllers do not establish useful certification at the task capability of leading AI systems.

sources.who: Xinhang Ma, Junlin Wu, Hussein Sibai, Yiannis Kantaros and Yevgeniy Vorobeychik
sources.showed: They trained controllers that act on camera images and obtained safety probability bounds. Their guarantees combine sampled starting conditions with all visual variations covered by a learned image model.
sources.quote:
the proposed
approach yields policies that exhibit significantly stronger

sources.cited_for: Useful performance and formal safety bounds can coexist in control tasks using images.
sources.not_established: Safety remains probabilistic over starting conditions and depends on assumptions about how well the image model covers real observations.

sources.who: Jeremy Cohen, Elan Rosenfeld and J. Zico Kolter
sources.showed: They proved guarantees for randomized smoothing, which combines predictions on randomly altered inputs. They applied it to full-resolution image recognition, with sampling-based confidence in the guarantees.
sources.quote:
In this paper, we prove the
ﬁrst tight robustness guarantee for randomized smoothing.
sources.cited_for: Large image-recognition models can retain useful performance while guaranteeing unchanged predictions under bounded input changes.
sources.not_established: Guaranteeing an unchanged image label under bounded changes does not establish broader task safety across useful deployment conditions.

sources.who: Guy Katz, Clark Barrett, David Dill, Kyle Julian and Mykel Kochenderfer
sources.showed: They built Reluplex, a tool for proving properties of learned networks, and proved rules governing advisories from prototype aircraft collision-avoidance networks.
sources.quote:
Additionally, we were able to prove
certain robustness properties [3] of the networks, meaning that small adversarial
perturbations do not change the advisories produced for certain inputs.
sources.cited_for: Specific behavioral rules can be proved for learned networks used in a substantive control task.
sources.not_established: These network-level properties do not establish complete-system safety or certification at the capability of leading AI systems.

shown: Chen and colleagues bounded a language-model safety detector's response to limited text changes. Teuber and colleagues went further toward complete control systems, proving safety without a time limit in some modeled aircraft scenarios.

Ma and colleagues combined useful camera-based control with safety probability bounds. These are narrower achievements than a computer-checked behavioral guarantee for a highly capable AI across useful operating conditions.
missing: A highly capable system must retain useful task performance while a guarantee covers enough of its intended use to matter.
A computer-checked proof must cover the deployed system, including any mechanism that declines to answer outside its guaranteed region.
The guarantee must account for declared changes in operating conditions, interventions and randomness.
Independent teams must be able to reproduce the guarantees and assess their practical operating costs.

milestones.label: Useful task performance against criteria declared in advance
milestones.explanation: A system would have to meet advance criteria for its task, operating conditions, guaranteed coverage and performance relative to a leading unconstrained model, without hidden human help. This makes usefulness measurable.

milestones.label: Computer-checked guarantees with useful performance and coverage
milestones.explanation: A computer-checked proof would have to cover the stated conditions, or every answer plus refusal outside the guaranteed region. The whole system must meet performance and coverage criteria so that refusing everything cannot qualify.

milestones.label: Reproducible proofs with explicit assumptions and costs
milestones.explanation: The system, rules, proofs and checks would have to support independent reproduction, with assumptions, access limits and operating costs explicit. This lets others assess whether the guarantee is usable in practice.

milestones.label: Substantive task guarantees within clearly stated limits
milestones.explanation: Certification would have to cover substantive task performance; a narrow text-change guarantee or an incapable network alone would not qualify. Independent reproduction across tasks would show breadth, while each proof keeps its stated scope.

uncertain: What performance gap from a leading model, guaranteed coverage and certification cost would count as useful for each task?
How can guarantees expand without erasing distinctions the task requires, when small text changes can legitimately change the correct judgment?
Which safety or correctness rules capture the intended outcome well enough for a proof to provide meaningful assurance?

page.title: AI systems with machine-checked behavioral guarantees
page.definition: An AI system adapted from a leading general-purpose model performs a specified task while a computer-checked proof establishes a behavioral property, or bounds its failure probability, for every input or initial condition in a declared operating model. The guarantee includes any safeguard or abstention mechanism.

goal.need: On 50 harmful AdvBench behaviours, four deterministic defenses across three language models retained 0–2% robustness against 20-token white-box suffix attacks. These attack results give upper bounds on robustness. A separate experiment certified a GPT-4o safety detector against an average of 2.02 token substitutions, using 1,000,000 samples and type-I error 0.01. This establishes local detector robustness rather than safety of every generated answer.

statements.body: Advanced Research + Invention Agency (ARIA), original Safeguarded AI programme
statements.quote: a viable and scalable path to safe transformative AI.
statements.context: The passage describes the intended consequence of demonstrating all three original technical areas: assurance infrastructure, verified learned systems and deployment.

statements.quote: to guarantee safety properties in adversarial environments
statements.context: The programme goal presented on 15 August 2017 concerns continual assurance of learning-enabled autonomous systems.

statements.quote: Our goal is to equip AI-produced code, control systems, and models with quantitative guarantees of correctness and fail-safety.
statements.context: The programme page records a May 2026 shift toward assurance tooling and cybersecurity.

completion.title: A deployed AI system combines task performance with a machine-checked behavioral guarantee.
completion.criterion: A system adapted from a leading general-purpose AI model operates in a production application and exceeds a non-certified baseline in both task performance and resilience to adverse events. A machine-checked proof establishes its specified behavioral property or risk bound for every allowed input or initial condition in its declared operating model, including the implemented controller and any safeguard or abstention logic. Abstentions count in task performance. The application fixes the benchmark, operating conditions and acceptable risk; this test supplies no numerical definition of frontier capability or minimum certified coverage.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas synthesis of ARIA's original simulation and production-deployment goals; no matching external acceptance standard was found.
completion.basis: Searched ARIA's original and revised programme materials, DARPA Assured Autonomy and NIST AI RMF for a joint test of frontier capability, certified coverage and machine checking; none defines one. NIST explicitly leaves risk tolerance application-specific. The proposed test combines ARIA's comparative performance target with its production-deployment goal. No cited result establishes the combined capability.

milestones.title: A neural network satisfies a specified input–output property for every input in its stated region.
milestones.criterion: Encode the network, allowed inputs and violation of the property as a satisfiability query. An UNSAT result establishes that no encoded counterexample exists. Katz et al. reported UNSAT for property φ1 on 41 of 45 ACAS Xu networks, with four timeouts; each network had 300 rectified linear units. Their floating-point implementation did not guarantee soundness, so these reported results do not constitute independently checked proof certificates.
milestones.set_by: Neural-network verification convention, applied by Katz et al. in Reluplex, Section 6 and Table 2.
milestones.threshold_quote: an UNSAT result indicates that a property holds

milestones.title: A classifier certifies an unchanged prediction within radius R with certification error at most α.
milestones.criterion: For a Gaussian-smoothed classifier g, except on a certification-sampling event of probability at most α, a returned class c and radius R guarantee g(x+δ)=c for every perturbation with ℓ₂ norm below R. The procedure can abstain. Cohen et al. reported 49% certified top-1 accuracy at radius 0.5 on 500 ImageNet images, using α=0.001. This is a sampling-qualified mathematical guarantee, rather than an inspected machine-checked proof. Chen et al.'s token-substitution detector certificates are a language-model application of local certification.
milestones.set_by: Certified-robustness convention, formalised by Cohen, Rosenfeld and Kolter in Proposition 2 and their certified-accuracy evaluation.
milestones.threshold_quote: With probability at least 1 − α over the randomness in CERTIFY

milestones.title: An independent checker with a proved soundness theorem accepts a neural-network proof certificate.
milestones.criterion: The checker validates every proof-tree split and leaf contradiction and returns true; its soundness theorem establishes that the encoded counterexample query has no satisfying assignment. Desmartin et al. implemented and proved such a checker in Imandra. Their evaluation certified all 276 collision-avoidance and 180 robot-navigation proofs selected for size below 5 MB. The result covers encoded queries; certified translation from higher-level task specifications remains outside that implementation.
milestones.set_by: Desmartin et al., Imandra certificate-checking protocol, Algorithm 1, Theorem 15 and Section 6.
milestones.threshold_quote: is certified if all checks pass.

milestones.title: A neural controller keeps its modelled physical system safe for arbitrarily many control cycles.
milestones.criterion: Prove that every execution from the allowed initial states satisfies the safety predicate after any number of controller–plant iterations, including continuous evolution. VerSAILLE Theorem 2 derives this from a valid control-envelope contract and an UNSAT neural-network refinement query. Teuber et al. demonstrated infinite-time safety for some Vertical Airborne Collision Avoidance scenarios; their largest verified networks had 270 rectified linear units. That aircraft analysis assumes zero intruder vertical velocity and excludes clear-of-conflict advisories.
milestones.set_by: Teuber, Mitsch and Platzer, VerSAILLE verification criterion, Theorem 2; the cited aircraft demonstration uses their stated benchmark restrictions.
milestones.threshold_quote: a dL proof on the infinite-time safety of the NNCS.

milestones.title: A verified controller beats non-certified baselines in simulated task performance and resilience.
milestones.criterion: In simulation, a learned controller for a complex application has verifiable quantitative probabilistic safety bounds and exceeds non-certified baselines in both task performance and resilience to adverse events. This is ARIA's original TA2 target. Related evidence from Ma et al.'s preprint covers four vision-control settings: finite-horizon safety bounds use 2,000 sampled initial states and confidence parameter δ=0.05. Those results do not establish this complete ARIA target or a production deployment.
milestones.set_by: ARIA, original Safeguarded AI programme thesis v1.2, TA2 target on page 7; a historical target preceding the May 2026 programme revision.
milestones.threshold_quote: achieves both better performance and better resilience to adverse events than non-certified baselines.

not_found: No external joint threshold for frontier task capability, certified deployment coverage and proof-checking cost was found in the ARIA, DARPA or NIST materials searched.
No independently replicated production demonstration satisfying the combined completion test was found.
Peer-review status for the cited Chen and Ma preprint versions was not established.

results.finding: Nine neural networks with 1–9 activation functions were verified for monotonicity.
results.detail: The prover checks each affine segment by solving a linear system encoding the input constraints and a property violation. Its guarantees use rational arithmetic; the benchmark networks were generated to be monotone.
results.quote:
For each network, we veriﬁed monotonicity ﬁve times and measured the
runtimes, as shown in Fig. 4.

results.finding: Imandra certified 100% of 456 selected neural-network verification proofs.
results.detail: The sample comprised 276 collision-avoidance and 180 robot-navigation proofs under 5 MB. The soundness theorem covers encoded queries; certified translation from higher-level specifications remains future work.
results.quote:
We evaluated the results of 276 coav and 180 robotics
queries, which have proof size smaller than 5MB. AllUNSAT proofs were checked by the
native Marabou checker and by Imandra, and both checkers have certified all queries.

results.finding: One modeled medical device with a neural controller was verified safe over an infinite time horizon.
results.detail: The proof uses Rocq and MathComp Analysis for the continuous system; neural-network properties are axiomatized in Rocq and justified by an external verifier. The Vehicle compiler is part of the trusted computing base.
results.quote:
Finally, to put the idea of
compositional neural-cyber-physical system verification
to the test, we use the Mathematical Components libraries in Rocq to verify infinite time-horizon safety of a medical device, modelled as a
continuous
cyber-physical system with a neural controller.

results.finding: Simulated quadrotor controller: sample size not stated; statistical verification sets a 1% violation-probability bound.
results.detail: The controller has a higher worst-case return and lower observed violation probability than the non-certified baselines. The text does not establish a direct simulation comparison with those baselines on resilience to adverse events. The bound applies to the sampled scenario distribution at 99% confidence.

results.finding: APTPchecker checked 93.7%–99.4% of generated proofs across a benchmark of 400 verification problems.
results.detail: The independent checker checks proof-tree structure and leaf infeasibility, and the paper gives a soundness argument. However, its LP solver is unverified, and symbolic checking of the implementation was depth-limited rather than an exhaustive soundness proof.
results.quote:
Overall, both verifiers were able to generate proofs for all problems with APTP, and APTPchecker is
able to check between 93.7% and 99.4% of the proofs that are generated.

results.finding: Rocq-NN-Roll verified monotonicity on 9 neural networks with 1–9 activation functions.
results.detail: The prover has a machine-checked soundness theorem and produces verification results itself. It does not independently check an external proof certificate or validate its proof-tree splits and leaf contradictions.
results.quote:
We evaluated the runtime on nine neural networks, 
each containing between one and nine activation functions.

results.finding: Imandra certified UNSAT proofs for all 456 evaluated collision-avoidance and robotics queries.
results.detail: The evaluated proofs covered 276 collision-avoidance and 180 robotics queries. The checker’s soundness was proved in Imandra; certified compilation from network specifications to queries remained future work.
results.quote:
We evaluated the results of 276 coav and 180 robotics
queries, which have proof size smaller than 5MB. AllUNSAT proofs were checked by the
native Marabou checker and by Imandra, and both checkers have certified all queries.

results.finding: Neural controllers for two simulated systems had a reported violation-probability bound of 1%.
results.detail: Statistical model checking used 1% error tolerance and 99% confidence over sampled scenario distributions. The assessment covers finite horizons, not a proof of safety for every execution over arbitrarily many cycles.
results.quote: Across both the standard and enlarged regions, Curr-ES and it robust version Curr-ES-R always satisfies safety constraints, demonstrating strong safety assurance and robust performance.

results.finding: Picid produced 94 valid UNSAT proofs among 180 ACAS Xu verification queries.
results.detail: The networks had 300 neurons. One additional UNSAT proof contained a hole. Proof production did not cover preprocessing, which requires separate analysis.

results.finding: DensePure achieved 77.8% certified accuracy at ℓ₂ radius 0.5 on ImageNet; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The paper reports randomized-smoothing certificates, but the supplied text does not state the certification-sampling error probability used in this experiment.

results.finding: A discrete adaptive cruise controller with 256 ReLU nodes was verified safe over an infinite horizon under perturbations of 0.01.
results.detail: One trained neural controller was verified against a safe control envelope. The guarantee applies to the declared model and bounded perturbations; a corresponding fixed-point implementation was synthesized.
results.quote:
For the chosen control envelope and idealized implementation we
veriﬁed safety under perturbation for at rained NN for δ = 
0.01 which simultaneously shows the envelope’sr obustness.
